lesson.title: Trading Rectangles for Trapezoids: The Trapezoidal Rule
lesson.summary: The trapezoidal rule replaces each rectangle with a trapezoid, which is exactly the same as averaging the left and right Riemann sums, and it is usually more accurate than either one alone.
lesson.body:
Every Riemann sum so far has approximated the area under a curve using flat topped rectangles. The trapezoidal rule instead uses trapezoids: over each subinterval, instead of one flat height, it connects the function's value at the left endpoint to its value at the right endpoint with a straight line, and computes the area of the resulting trapezoid. A trapezoid with parallel sides of length f(x_(i-1)) and f(x_i) and width Δx has area Δx times [f(x_(i-1))+f(x_i)] divided by 2, the average of the two heights times the width.

Summing that formula across all n subintervals and simplifying gives the trapezoidal rule in its usual compact form: (Δx/2) times [f(x0) + 2f(x1) + 2f(x2) + ... + 2f(x_(n-1)) + f(xn)], where every interior partition point gets counted twice, since it is the right edge of one trapezoid and the left edge of the next, and only the two outermost points are counted once. There is a second, equally useful way to see this rule: it is exactly the average of the left Riemann sum and the right Riemann sum computed on the same partition. That is not a coincidence, it falls straight out of the fact that a trapezoid's area is the average of its two parallel sides times its width, matching how the left and right sums each contribute one of those two sides.

Use the same f(x) = x² on the interval from 0 to 2, n = 4, Δx = 0.5, with the left sum, 1.75, and right sum, 3.75, already computed in the previous two chapters. The trapezoidal estimate is the average of those two: (1.75+3.75)/2 = 2.75. You can also get this directly from the compact formula: (0.5/2) times [f(0) + 2f(0.5) + 2f(1.0) + 2f(1.5) + f(2.0)] = 0.25 times [0 + 2(0.25) + 2(1.0) + 2(2.25) + 4.0] = 0.25 times [0+0.5+2.0+4.5+4.0] = 0.25 times 11 = 2.75. Both methods agree, as they must.

Compare the trapezoidal estimate of 2.75 to the exact value, 8/3, about 2.6667: the error is about 0.0833, better than either the left sum's error of about 0.9167 or the right sum's error of about 1.0833, but not as good as the midpoint sum's error of about 0.0417 from the previous chapter. This ordering, midpoint beating trapezoidal, beating left and right, is typical, though not universal, for smooth curving functions like x squared. When a quick, more accurate estimate is needed and only endpoint data is available, the trapezoidal rule is the natural first upgrade over a plain left or right sum, but the midpoint rule is often the better choice when you are free to pick your own sample points.

The trapezoidal rule builds on the general Riemann sum framework the same way the other three do, but it is worth noticing it does not fit the pick one sample point per subinterval mold the others follow, it blends two sample points, the two endpoints, into a single estimate per subinterval instead. That makes it a natural bridge between simple Riemann sums and more advanced numerical integration techniques that come later in a calculus sequence.
